newsitem.title: USA: Maine court rejects most of referendum challenge.
newsitem.headline: Maine court rejects most of referendum challenge.

text.p: Maine's State Supreme Court rejected all but one of the arguments raised by Family Forestry Coalition seeking to knock off the November ballot Gov. Angus King's proposal to limit clearcutting in forests.

The group argued the legislature violated the constitution by putting the measure on the ballot. King recalled the legislature to approve his alternative to a competing proposal that would ban clearcutting entirely.

The justices disagreed with Family Forestry Coalition, finding the wording of the question was not misleading and lawmakers acted lawfully. However, the court left open the possibility of a future challenge to provisions of King's measure affecting public lands.
The justices said that if voters approve the governor's proposal, called the compact for Maine forests, they will consider a challenge to that portion of the measure.

An indication of how high the stakes are in the fight over how the state's forests will be handled, Maine Citizens for a Healthy Forest and Economy set a new record for fundraising for a ballot question.

The campaign group has raised about $5.5 million, with the lion's share of the funds coming from the paper industry. This spending exceeds the 1987 record of $4.3 million spent in the referendum to close the Maine Yankee Nuclear Plant.

Supporters of the Ban Clearcutting referendum have raised just over $400,000. And the third group, which is fighting both King's compact and the outright ban has raised just $30,000. By the time the voters select one of these options at the Nov 5 elections, the total amount on the three competing measures could hit $6.5 million.

While a poll earlier this week by Strategic Marketing Survey showed that 46 percent of those polled said they will vote for governor's measure, thousands of students across the state who later were polled were not as supportive.

In a mock election sponsored by the Maine Secretary of State, just under 50 percent of the students at 488 schools supported King's measure to limit clearcutting, while the measure that would entirely ban clearcutting got nearly 35-percent of the votes.
A little more than 15 percent opposed both proposals to change forest practices.
Under the state constitution, one of the three options must get more than half the vote or the questions getting most support must go to the voters in a special referendum.
